conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode; 'session' means one trading day of intraday bars; standard Brooks setups referenced only by name (high 1/high 2, moving-average gap bar, wedge, head-and-shoulders flag, expanding triangle, two-bar reversal) are primitives from earlier chapters and are not redefined here

candidates.name: AverageDailyRangeHistory
candidates.quote: The protracted trading range is often a very tight trading range.
candidates.description: Primitive with state: maintain a rolling average of the last M completed sessions' full-day range (high-low), for use in judging whether the current session's midday range is unusually tight.
candidates.pseudocode: newSession = Date(0) != Date(1); if (newSession) { pushDailyRange(sessionHigh - sessionLow); sessionHigh = high[0]; sessionLow = low[0] } else { sessionHigh = max(sessionHigh, high[0]); sessionLow = min(sessionLow, low[0]) } avgDailyRange = average(lastNDailyRanges, dayLookback)

complexity.reason: needs session-boundary detection and a rolling multi-day range history built from intraday bars

notes: Lighter version of the opening-range primitives in chapters 22-24 (no opening-range-specific fields needed here).

candidates.name: MorningTrendLegFlag
candidates.quote: The day has a strong trend in the first hour or so and then enters a trading range.
candidates.description: Primitive with state: a session flag, set when the net move over the first N bars of the session (close of bar N minus session open) exceeds a size threshold; records the direction and the leg's height for later comparison.
candidates.pseudocode: newSession: morningLegDirection = 0; if (barsIntoSession == firstHourBars) { morningLegHeight = abs(close[0] - sessionOpen); if (morningLegHeight >= minLegAtr * atr) morningLegDirection = sign(close[0] - sessionOpen) }

complexity.reason: per-session state anchored at a fixed bar count

candidates.name: TightMiddayRangePredictsResumption
candidates.quote: Whenever this happens and especially if the sideways action is in a very tight trading range, the day is likely becoming a trend resumption day.
candidates.description: Filter: after a qualifying morning trend leg (T25-02), the market has stayed inside a tight range for at least H hours; the tighter that midday range relative to the average daily range, the more likely a late-session resumption of the morning trend. Enables the trap-fade (T25-04) and blocks new countertrend entries.
candidates.pseudocode: morningLegDirection != 0 && barsSinceMorningLeg >= minMiddayBars && (middayRangeHigh - middayRangeLow) <= tightRangeFraction * avgDailyRange

complexity.reason: combines two stateful primitives plus a running midday range measurement

notes: Page 454: the midday action does not have to be a flat range -- a weakly trending countertrend move for a couple of hours that ultimately fails is a variant of this same setup; tightRangeFraction is a proxy for either form.

candidates.name: FailedReversalBreakoutTrapFade
candidates.quote: There is often a breakout from the trading range late in the day that tries to reverse the trend, but it is usually a trap. The market then reverses and breaks out in the opposite direction into the close. A trap is more likely when the trading range is unusually tight.
candidates.description: Entry (mirrored to the long side, for a morning bull trend that pulled into a tight range): a late-session breakout beyond the midday range in the direction OPPOSITE the morning trend fails within a few bars (price closes back inside the range); buy at the next open, expecting the trend-resumption breakout the other way.
candidates.pseudocode: tightMiddayRangeSetup && morningLegDirection == 1 && low[failBars..1] < middayRangeLow /* opposite-direction breakout occurred */ && close[0] > middayRangeLow
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the failure bar (or the reversal bar that closes back inside the range)

complexity.reason: requires the tight-midday-range state plus a breakout-then-failure scan

notes: Page 454: this trap breakout often occurs between 11 a.m. and noon PST; a Time gate could tighten this further.

candidates.name: MiddayThreePushCountertrendLikelyFails
candidates.quote: Sometimes there are three countertrend lazy pushes, creating a wedge flag. At other times the third leg fails to surpass the second, and this forms a head and shoulders flag (most head and shoulders reversal patterns fail and become continuation patterns).
candidates.description: Filter: during the midday range following a morning trend leg, a developing three-push countertrend pattern (wedge or head-and-shoulders shaped) is more likely to fail and resume the original trend than to become a genuine reversal; bias against fading the morning trend on this pattern and prefer resuming with-trend entries once it fails.

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot / three-push detection restricted to the midday window

candidates.name: MultiDayTrendResumptionBreakout
candidates.quote: Trend resumption patterns often take place over two or more days...Trading ranges can last a long time, but usually break out in the direction of the trend.
candidates.description: Filter: after a strong multi-session trend leg, price has since stayed inside that leg's range (has not retraced past a fraction of it) for up to K sessions; a breakout beyond the range's edge, in the leg's original direction, is a high-conviction trend-resumption entry regardless of how many sessions the pause lasted.
candidates.pseudocode: priorLegDirection != 0 && sessionsSincePriorLeg <= maxPauseSessions && retracementSincePriorLeg <= maxRetraceFraction * priorLegHeight && close[0] > pauseRangeHigh  /* long side */
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop above the pause range's high

complexity.reason: cross-session state tracked over many sessions, remembering a leg's direction, height, and the pause range it settled into

notes: Page 460's example resumed a bear leg five sessions after the first move down; the pause need not be a single tight box the whole time.

candidates.name: SpikeHeightMeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: Any breakout often is followed by a measured move based on the spike. It is usually based on the height from the open or low of the first bar of the spike to the close or high of the final bar.
candidates.description: Exit/target: for a long entered on (or during) a breakout spike, project a measured-move target using the spike's own height -- from the open or low of the spike's first bar to the close or high of its final bar -- added onto the breakout point.
candidates.pseudocode: spikeHeight = (useBody ? close[spikeEndBar] : high[spikeEndBar]) - (useBody ? open[spikeStartBar] : low[spikeStartBar]); target = breakoutPoint + moveMultiple * spikeHeight; ctx.MarketPosition() > 0 && high[0] >= target
candidates.book_order_type: limit order at the measured-move target

complexity.reason: reads the remembered spike-state extremes (as in T21-07/T21-13) and does arithmetic

notes: Same measured-move idea as T21-13/T22-05/T23-18; this instance is anchored to a two-bar breakout spike specifically.

candidates.name: RepeatedLevelTestHoldsIsStrength
candidates.quote: Notice how the market repeatedly tested the support line at the bar 7 low to the tick and continued to find buyers...The market ran the stops below that entry bar by one tick, but, despite many attempts, it could not go any further down. This is a sign of strong bulls at work.
candidates.description: Filter: a support (or resistance) level is tested at least K times within a lookback window, each test holding at or within a small tolerance of the level without a bar closing meaningfully beyond it; repeated holds strengthen confidence in that level and favor with-trend entries off it over fading a break of it.
candidates.pseudocode: touchCount = count over k in 0..lookback-1 of (low[k] <= level + toleranceAtr * atr && close[k] > level - breakToleranceAtr * atr); touchCount >= minTouches

complexity.reason: requires a remembered support/resistance level plus a windowed touch-count test

rejected.quote: You can never be certain and there is always about a 40 percent chance that the exact opposite can happen.
rejected.reason: a discretionary base-rate observation, not a bar-level test

chapter_summary: Chapter 25 covers the trend resumption day: a strong opening trend, a long (often very tight) midday trading range that lulls traders, and a resumption of the original trend into the close, frequently preceded by a failed reversal breakout trap. Minable material centers on detecting the setup (a morning trend-leg flag plus a tight-midday-range measurement against the average daily range), trading the trap (fading a failed countertrend breakout back into the original direction, and discounting apparent three-push wedge/head-and-shoulders reversals during the range), a measured-move exit target sized from the resumption spike, and a general 'repeated level test holds' strength signal. The pattern is explicitly noted to also occur across multiple sessions, which is captured as a separate cross-session breakout filter.
